entities.summary: James Richmond Barthé, also known as Richmond Barthé was an African-American sculptor associated with the Harlem Renaissance. Barthé is best known for his portrayal of black subjects. The focus of his artistic work was portraying the diversity and spirituality of man. Barthé once said: "All my life I have been interested in trying to capture the spiritual quality I see and feel in people, and I feel that the human figure as God made it, is the best means of expressing this spirit in man.". Richmond Barthé was a authors & novelists from Bay St. Louis (1901-01-28, Bay St. Louis–1989-03-06). A moderately significant entity in the historical record. Relevant to cause-and-effect analysis.

entities.summary:
James Richmond Barthé, a seminal African-American sculptor, profoundly shaped the visual arts of the Harlem Renaissance and beyond, establishing himself as a master of figurative art from the 1920s through the mid-20th century. Born in Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, in 1901, Barthé dedicated his career to capturing the inherent dignity and spiritual essence of the human form, with a particular emphasis on Black subjects. His work transcended mere portraiture, aiming to articulate the universal human experience through the nuanced portrayal of identity, emotion, and physicality, thereby challenging prevailing racial stereotypes and elevating Black representation in fine art.

After initially studying painting at the Art Institute of Chicago, Barthé transitioned to sculpture, recognizing its capacity for three-dimensional expression. His early success in Chicago led to a crucial move to New York City in 1929, where he became a vital contributor to the Harlem Renaissance's artistic flourishing. During this period, Barthé produced iconic works such as 'Stevedore' (1937), a powerful depiction of a Black laborer, and 'Exodus' (1929), which explored themes of migration and identity. His sculptures, often rendered in bronze, terra cotta, and plaster, were celebrated for their classical elegance, dynamic movement, and profound psychological depth, earning him commissions for public monuments and widespread critical acclaim.
